This method extracts intensity information from a few spatially distributed points in a speckle plane, where object feature is naturally multiplexed, thereby transforming scattering from a detrimental effect into an efficient encoding mechanism while drastically reducing sampling requirements. Remarkably, it achieves over 99% retrieval accuracy for OAMs recognition using just 16 sampling points, corresponding to a sampling density of 0.024% compared with conventional imaging-based approaches. Furthermore, spatiotemporally interleaved vortex beams decoding, high-capacity OAM-multiplexed communication, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST classification are implemented to verify the versatility of SMPD. This work establishes a scalable strategy for efficient optical information processing and fiber-based sensing in complex environments.

---

## Introduction

The precise manipulation of light’s orbital angular momentum (OAM) phase dependence of exp(iℓθ), enables robust encoding of information into discrete OAM modes. These modes form the backbone of spatial multiplexing strategies that transcend classical transmission limits1–3.

To decode OAM modes, approaches such as interferometry19–21, vortex diffraction grating22–24, and machine learning25,26 have proven effective in free-space environments. While demonstrating success, they generally depend on high-resolution imaging to capture well-defined full-field light structures, necessitating thousands of pixels or more and computationally intensive processing. Such reliance on dense spatial sampling imposes stringent trade-offs; it throttles system bandwidth, complicates scalability, and obstructs real-time operation27,28. Consequently, applications demanding compact form factors, high-speed detection, or operation in photon-limited scenarios, cornerstones of next-generation photonic technologies, remain largely out of reach.

Recent advances reveal that the ostensibly disordered nature of speckle fields marks a profound redundancy in their information content29–31. Unlike direct imaging systems, which localize spatial information to discrete regions, multiple scattering in complex media redistributes input-field contributions across the entire speckle pattern (see Supplementary Note 1 for more details). This non-local encoding enables information retrieval based on partial-field sampling for tasks such as imaging through scattering media32, diffuser-based super-resolution imaging via sub-Nyquist sampling33, and OAM recognition5,9,34–36 from arbitrary speckle subregions.

Yet, leveraging this redundancy for ultra-low-sampling detection remains underexplored. Although indeed utilizing a portion of the speckle field, current implementations still often rely on capturing a high-resolution intensity profile pattern (comprising thousands to millions of data points). A pivot challenge persists: What constitutes the minimal spatial sampling required to maintain accurate, scalable mode discrimination?

To address this, we propose spatially multiplexed points detection (SMPD), a framework for single-shot pattern classification with unprecedented sampling efficiency. Instead of recording full-field speckles, SMPD spatially samples intensity fluctuations at a sparse array of spatially multiplexed single-pixel detectors (SPDs), each capturing globally encoded information from the scattered field. A custom-designed neural network deciphers these sub-Nyquist intensity sequences, achieving robust OAM recognition with a sampling density of 0.024%, 4096 times lower than conventional imaging-based methods, while maintaining over 99% accuracy in diversity OAM recognition scenarios. Beyond OAM-mode retrieval, SMPD generalizes to classify mode-dependent features and distinguish complex optical fields, including handwritten digit recognition, grayscale images of clothing classification, and axicon angle identification, demonstrating its versatility across diverse scenarios.

By refining the spatial sampling-information capability trade-off, SMPD transcends the limitation of imaging-centric detection paradigms. This approach enables high-dimensional optical sensing and communication systems that are both compact and bandwidth-efficient, critical for real-time operation in photon-starved environments. Furthermore, its ultralow sampling requirements may unlock applications for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) sensing, low-power LIDAR, and quantum-enhanced sensing, where conventional pixel-dense sensors, constrained by their limited bandwidth and spectral ranges, prove impractical. SMPD thus establishes a pathway toward scalable photonic technologies, bridging the gap between theoretical information redundancy and practical, resource-efficient detection.

Figure 1 illustrates the concept of SMPD, where two orthogonally polarized vortex beams transmitted through a multimode fiber (MMF) generate a speckle pattern at the distal end of the fiber. Instead of conventional full-field imaging, SMPD employs spatially distributed SPDs to sample sparse intensity points. These measurements are processed by a customized neural network termed as Recognizing OAM Artificial Neural Network (ROAM-ANN), which secures two paths to extract the features of the inputs in different dimensions and eventually outputs the encoded OAMs from the pointwise intensity sequences.

Here, SPD is defined in units of ‘px’, and 1 px corresponds to the area of a single element (7.42 μm2) in the CCD camera. For instance, an SPD area of 52 px indicates 5 by 5 neighboring CCD elements are combined to form one SPD, and a total of 9 points mean that 9 such SPDs are imposed on the detecting plane via the mask. As seen, 16 SPDs (each spanning 30 × 30 px) achieved >99% accuracy for both OAM modes. Critically, the total sampling density of this configuration is approximately 0.024% (16 vs. 256 × 256), corresponding to 4096 times lower than that of conventional imaging-based methods9 that usually require 256 × 256 or more pixel arrays. Even with SPDs reduced to 2 × 2 px (retaining 16 detectors), accuracy remained above 93%.

That said, a clear trade-off emerged between SPD count and SPD size: reducing either the number of sampling points (which is critical for capturing multiplexed information and speckle correlations) or the sensing area (which helps resist perturbations and avoids sampling low-intensity or uninformative zones, as further discussed in Supplementary Note 1.4) led to degraded performance. For instance, with only 6 SPDs (1 × 1 px), accuracy dropped below 50%, highlighting the necessity of using sufficient sampling points and an adequately large sensing area to ensure robust performance, mitigate noise, and reduce sensitivity to pixel displacement. In addition to recognizing orthogonally polarized vortex beams, we also conducted simulations involving pairs of linearly polarized vortex beams with varying polarization angle differences (see details in Supplementary Note 6). However, in practical scenarios, such as with speckles generated by a small-core MMF, a strong scrambled condition is difficult to achieve. Sparse sampling, by contrast, collects information from more uncorrelated regions of the speckle field and thus significantly improves reconstruction accuracy.

It remains effective whether the speckle grains are large (indicative of insufficient scattering) or small (indicative of strong scattering), offering broad applicability and better practical performance under varying physical conditions.

Figure 3 illustrates the conceptual framework of the experiment (see Supplementary Note 3 for details). In this context, an input consists of eight distinct OAM modes, and a prediction is considered correct only if all eight are accurately classified. Using 49 sampling points (i.e., a 7 × 7 SPD array), the collective recognition accuracy reaches 98.6%, indicating highly reliable multi-mode detection. To further address the reviewers’ concerns regarding the originality of the proposed method, an additional decoding experiment using SMPD is conducted to resolve spatiotemporal superimposed vortex beams. In this experiment, SMPD is employed to simultaneously decode eight vortex beams whose OAM values are randomly distributed between 2.1 and 2.8. These beams are sequentially transmitted through an MMF, and their intensities are spatiotemporally superimposed, resulting in a composite speckle pattern that encodes all eight beams. We demonstrate the versatility of SMPD in spatiotemporal resolving by exploiting the redundancy of spatial speckle field.
Figure R3 illustrates the conceptual framework of the experiment. Each vortex beam, carrying a randomly selected OAM value alongside their corresponding temporal phase masks, is transmitted through the MMF in chronological order. At the distal end of the MMF, a CCD camera captures a single speckle image representing the superposition of the eight individual speckle patterns. This process is synchronized using a function generator, which triggers the DMD eight times and the camera once during each acquisition cycle.

Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the interpretation of pixel density, sparsity, and the role of sampling in our approach. We fully agree that, under the condition of sufficiently strong scattering, as long as the sampling satisfies the Nyquist criterion, any selection of regions—whether proximal or scattered—should contain comparable information content. This is a valid and important observation. That said, practical systems face constraints associated with a) sensor density within the sampling regions, which impacts local noise robustness, and b) spatial sparsity of the sampling regions, which helps mitigate redundancy by capturing uncorrelated speckle grains.
The reviewer’s opinion holds well in the idealized case of strong scattering, where speckle grains are small and densely distributed. But in scenarios involving insufficient scattering, such as with multi-mode fibers (MMFs) of small cores, the output exhibits larger grain sizes and proximal sampling becomes highly redundant. In such cases, scattered sampling significantly improves reconstruction accuracy, as it captures more independent speckle information. More importantly, scattered sampling is robust across both regimes: it performs well regardless the size of the speckle grains, thus offering broader applicability and better performance across various physical conditions.
We have incorporated both the reviewer’s perspective and our extended discussion—covering the influence of sampling density, spatial sparsity, and speckle characteristics—into the revised manuscript to provide a more balanced and comprehensive analysis. Detailed mathematical analysis and experimental validation are also presented in the following sections for your information: 2.1 Pixel Density within Sampling Regions, 2.2 Sparsity of Sampling Regions across the Speckle Field, and 2.3 Experimental Validation.
2.1 Pixel Density within Sampling Regions
There are two practical considerations that justify the use of higher pixel density in a given sampling region: noise reduction and sampling effectiveness in sparse speckle fields. In theory, a single pixel in each sampling region is effective. However, in practice, individual pixels are susceptible to noise from various sources, such as mechanical vibrations (causing pixel displacement) or sensor noise (e.g., dark current). Sampling over a denser pixel region helps to average out such noise, thereby increasing the reliability and stability of the recorded intensity.
Fig. S2 Different categories presents similar intensity distribution in the output field: (a) the speckle pattern of two encoded pixels (gray value of 102 and 189, respectively); (b) the difference between the two speckle patterns.
As shown in Fig. S2a in the supplementary, the speckle field distribution is inherently random and sparse, with large areas exhibiting zero or near-zero intensity due to destructive interference. This sparsity means that if a sampling region is too small, there is a significant chance it may fall in a low-intensity or uninformative zone. A higher pixel density (corresponding to a larger active area) increases the likelihood of capturing useful information embedded in the speckle pattern.
Thus, while a single pixel may theoretically suffice, a higher-density (larger area) sampling region provides practical robustness and ensures greater information reliability, especially under real-world conditions.

Response:
We fully appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the classification of optically encoded non-orthogonal data, such as handwritten digits. Indeed, unlike orthogonal mode sets like orbital angular momentum (OAM) and polarization, digit-shaped fields significantly overlap in the transverse plane, making them inherently more challenging to distinguish. The fact that our method achieves high classification accuracy under such conditions demonstrates its robustness and highlights its potential for structured-light-based recognition in complex, real-world scenarios.
As mentioned in the additional simulations (1.3 Additional Experiments Part 1), the proposed SMPD method can successfully distinguish between overlapping vortex beams with a polarization angle difference as small as 5°, achieving recognition accuracy of approximately 90%. These results confirm that the proposed method is not only capable of recognizing digit-shaped fields but is also effective in resolving non-orthogonal structured-light fields with fine polarization variations. This reinforces the general applicability and robustness of our technique in complex optical encoding scenarios.
To further demonstrate the versatility of our method in non-orthogonal domains, we also conducted a simulation using the Fashion-MNIST dataset to classify grayscale images of clothing. Three configurations were tested for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST: 7 × 7, 6 × 6, and 5 × 5 arrays, where each detector integrates intensity over a 10 × 10 px region. This results in sparse sequences of 49, 36, or 25 intensity values per image. The dataset of 60,000 samples was split into training, validation, and test sets in an 8:1:1 ratio.
Remarkably, SMPD achieved 92%, 89.45%, and 83.28% recognition accuracy on the MNIST test dataset (6,000 samples) for 7 × 7, 6 × 6, and 5 × 5 SPD arrays, respectively (Fig. R8b). The confusion matrices (Fig. R8c) reveal minimal misclassification trends, with errors predominantly occurring between morphologically similar digits (e.g., 3↔5, 4↔9).
On the Fashion-MNIST test set, which contains 6,000 intensities sequences, SMPD achieved test accuracies of approximately 84%, 82%, and 81% for each SPD configuration. As shown in the confusion matrix (Fig. R8c), misclassifications primarily occurred among upper-body clothing items—such as shirts, T-shirts, pullovers, and coats—due to their high visual similarity, examples of which are illustrated in Fig. R8a.
These results confirm that spatially sparse, non-locally encoded speckle measurements encapsulate sufficient information for high-accuracy classification across diverse, non-orthogonal image sets, without resorting to pixel-dense sensors. By reducing sensor-pixel requirements to an extremely low subsampling rate (e.g., 5 × 5 arrays vs. 28× 28 pixels, 3.19% sampling density), SMPD offers a computationally efficient, hardware-lean pathway to deploy optical classifiers in scenarios where pixel-dense cameras are impractical or where speed, power and footprint are at a premium.

2. Figure 2 indicates that increasing both the number and area of SPDs improves recognition accuracy. In practical applications, how should this trade-off be optimized or balanced?
Response:
To better visualize the influence of the number and area of SPDs on recognition accuracy, we conducted a series of simulations. In these simulations, two vortex beams (with polarization angles of 30° and 70°, respectively) carrying either the same or different orbital angular momentum (OAM) values were transmitted through a MMF, generating speckle patterns at the output. The grain size of the resulting speckle field was set to 6 pixels. To evaluate the impact of different sampling strategies, we applied masks with varying sampling areas (i.e., pixel densities) and spatial sparsity to the speckle field. Each mask contained 16 SPDs, with configurations varying in both spatial sparsity (wide vs. narrow distribution) and pixel density (from 6×6 down to 1×1). The profiles and corresponding recognition accuracies are summarized in Table R5.

As shown in Table R5, when the sampling area is smaller than the SGS (e.g., 2×2 pixels), a wider spatial deployment of SPDs yields noticeably better recognition performance than a narrow deployment does. However, when the sampling area exceeds the SGS (e.g., 6×6 pixels), both wide and narrow deployments achieve comparably high recognition accuracies, outperforming configurations with smaller sampling areas. Notably, when the sampling area is reduced to 1×1 pixels, recognition accuracy drops significantly. As mentioned above, this is attributed to the higher probability of sampling in intensity-null or low-information regions, due to the limited spatial footprint of individual detectors.
In practical applications, this trade-off can be solved by considering two perspectives: SGS of the speckle field and effective sampling points. As mentioned earlier, the sampling area of each detector should ideally be larger than half the SGS. This ensures that each SPD captures meaningful intensity information, rather than noise or null regions. Furthermore, the minimum spatial distance between SPDs should be larger than the SGS to reduce spatial correlation and capture diverse speckle features. On ther other hand, while a larger sampling area helps improve robustness and noise resistance, the total number of SPDs plays a more critical role in capturing a broader range of usable information. Therefore, increasing the number of well-distributed SPDs generally yields greater improvements in recognition accuracy than merely increasing their size.
In conclusion, for optimal system design, the detector size should be matched to the SGS (preferably slightly larger), and the SPDs should be distributed with sufficient spacing to avoid redundancy. Under constraints on the number of detectors, maximizing spatial coverage (i.e., using a wide distribution) can significantly improve recognition performance.

4. As environmental vibrations are inevitable in real-world settings, it is important to assess the impact of speckle pattern translations on recognition accuracy. How sensitive is the system to such perturbations, and what is its robustness threshold?
Response:
To assess the system’s robustness against environmental perturbations, we conducted a series of simulations focusing on two main types of disturbances: linear translations—referred to as "speckle moving width"—of 2 and 4 pixels, and rotational shifts randomly ranging from 0° to 3°. These simulations were performed under a variety of configurations, including different speckle grain sizes (SGS), sampling areas, and numbers of sampling points.
Tables R7–R11 summarize the recognition accuracy for two OAM states under different speckle moving widths (2 and 4 pixels), SGS (6 and 16), and sampling areas (102~302).
When the speckle moving width was limited to 2 pixels, recognition accuracy experienced only a minor decline. For instance, with SGS set to 6 and a sampling area of 102 pixels, the accuracy for OAM1 and OAM2 was 75.1% and 70.0%, respectively. As the sampling area increased to 302 pixels, the accuracy improved significantly, reaching 88.5% and 88.6%. This trend was even more pronounced when using a larger SGS of 16, where the accuracy under the same conditions rose to 93.7% for OAM1 and 92.7% for OAM2. These findings highlight that both a larger sampling area and a larger SGS can effectively mitigate the impact of minor translations.
However, when the speckle moving width increased to 4 pixels, the system’s performance exhibited more noticeable degradation, particularly with smaller sampling areas and lower SGS. For example, under SGS = 6 and a 102 pixel sampling area, recognition accuracy dropped to 56.3% for OAM1 and 47.3% for OAM2. Nevertheless, increasing the sampling area to 302 pixels raised the accuracy to over 70% for both states. The use of a larger SGS (16) significantly improved robustness in these cases as well. Even at a 4-pixel displacement, accuracy for OAM1 and OAM2 reached 79.1% and 83.4%, respectively, with a 302 pixel sampling area. Larger SGS (16) provides greater robustness to speckle translation, as larger speckle grains are less sensitive to small positional shifts.
Further analysis demonstrated that increasing the number of sampling points also enhances resilience to translation. In scenarios with a 4-pixel speckle moving width and SGS = 16, increasing the sampling points from 25 to 36 yielded noticeable improvements. For instance, with a 202 pixel sampling area, recognition accuracy improved from 89.0% to 92.5% for OAM1, and from 88.3% to 92.7% for OAM2. This suggests that denser sampling can effectively compensate for inaccurate measurement caused by larger displacements and reinforce the system’s robustness.

5. The recognition accuracy for OAM2 is consistently lower than that for OAM1 by ~10%. What causes this difference? Is it related to the intrinsic properties of the OAM states, their spatial frequency content, or potential overlaps in speckle features?
Response:
Thaks a lot for noticing the details. The observed difference in recognition accuracy between OAM1 and OAM2 can be attributed to a combination of experimental imperfections and slight misalignments in the optical setup. These differences are not primarily due to the intrinsic properties of the OAM states themselves, but rather to practical factors affecting the generation and coupling of the vortex beams.
Firstly, imperfections in the experimental components, such as the half-wave plate and polarizing beam splitter, contribute to discrepancies in the intensity and quality of the two vortex beams. Manufacturing tolerances and non-ideal optical coatings can result in uneven polarization modulation and splitting efficiency, which in turn causes variations in the output intensity of the two beams. Since the proposed recognition method relies heavily on the intensity distribution of the speckle patterns, such differences can lead to unbalanced datasets and reduced recognition performance for the lower-intensity beam—typically OAM2 in this case.
Secondly, the optical alignment of the two vortex beams introduces another source of asymmetry. The system requires independent modulation of each beam using separate spatial light modulators (SLMs), followed by coupling into the same MMF. This process involves multiple reflective and refractive adjustments, making it difficult to achieve identical coupling efficiency for both beams. Even slight deviations in beam alignment or focus can lead to differences in the resulting speckle patterns, further contributing to the accuracy gap between OAM1 and OAM2.
In summary, the lower recognition accuracy for OAM2 is primarily due to experimental factors. That includes non-ideal optical components and imperfect alignment during beam modulation and coupling, but not fundamental differences in the spatial frequency content or intrinsic properties of the OAM states. Addressing these issues through improved component quality and more precise alignment procedures may help reduce the recognition gap between different OAM channels.
6. Under the current experimental conditions, what is the finest OAM resolution (i.e., minimal discernible OAM spacing) that can be reliably achieved? What factors fundamentally limit this resolution?
Response:
Under the current experimental conditions, the finest reliably achievable OAM resolution is approximately 0.1. This means that the system can distinguish between two OAM states whose topological charges differ by as small as 0.1. In contrast, simulations suggest that the system has the potential to achieve an even finer resolution of down to 0.01 under ideal, noise-free conditions. In simulation tests where the topological charges of two vortex beams varied continuously from 1.00 to 1.99, the recognition accuracy reached 99.4% for OAM1 and 99.9% for OAM2, demonstrating the method’s theoretical capability to resolve extremely fine differences in OAM.
However, achieving this level of resolution experimentally is significantly more challenging due to the presence of noise and imperfections in the optical system. Under current conditions, a resolution of 0.1 represents a reliable and achievable benchmark for OAM discrimination.
7. When using 9 or 16 SPDs (with 1 px area), the recognition accuracy falls below 90%, yet the OAM multiplexed transmission accuracy exceeds 93%. The authors should explain this discrepancy.
Response:
This discrepancy arises primarily from two key differences between the experimental setups: light source stability and speckle grain size (SGS).
a) Light source stability
Experiment 1 employed a sub-femtosecond pulsed laser (Origami-10XP, 1028 nm central wavelength, 400 fs pulse duration, 1 MHz repetition rate). Experiment 2 used a continuous-wave (CW) laser (EXLSR-532-300-CDRH, Spectra Physics, USA). The former one, the pulsed laser, is inherently more sensitive to environmental fluctuations such as temperature, vibration, and power supply instability. These factors lead to variations in the average power and output intensity of the speckle patterns. Since the recognition method relies on ultra-sparse intensity sampling, even minor fluctuations can introduce inconsistencies in the dataset, degrading recognition accuracy. In contrast, the CW laser used in Experiment 2 provides a more stable output, leading to more consistent speckle intensity profiles and improved recognition performance. As a result, Experiment 1 requires more SPDs or a larger sampling area to compensate for the instability of the light source.
b) Speckle grain size (SGS)
As discussed in Responses 1–3, SGS significantly influences the recognition accuracy. In this study, Experiment 1 used a MMF with a 62.5 µm core diameter, resulting in larger speckle grains. Experiment 2 used a MMF with a 200 µm core diameter, producing smaller speckle grains. When the detector area is much smaller than the SGS, sampling becomes more susceptible to noise and less representative of the overall speckle pattern. In Experiment 1, the larger SGS reduces the effectiveness of sparse sampling with 1 px SPDs, leading to lower recognition accuracy. Furthermore, larger SGSs are generally more sensitive to positional shifts, reducing robustness in practical setups.
8. Given that multimode fibers (MMFs) are sensitive to environmental factors such as temperature and airflow, which reportedly limit data stability to ~30 minutes, the authors are encouraged to discuss potential mitigation strategies.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the practical limitations imposed by the environmental sensitivity of MMFs. Indeed, unmitigated fluctuations in temperature, airflow, and mechanical stress can alter the fiber’s transmission matrix and hence the speckle patterns, compromising data stability over extended periods. To address these challenges, we propose the following mitigation strategies:
a) Periodic reference calibration: By intermittently injecting a known reference beam (e.g., a Gaussian mode) and recording its speckle fingerprint, we can track slow drifts in the transmission matrix and apply a real-time correction to the classifier inputs.
b) Sliding-Window training: Implementing an adaptive classifier that continuously updates its training set using only the most recent data can compensate for gradual changes, effectively “retraining on the fly” to maintain accuracy beyond 30 minutes.
c) Data augmentation with perturbations: During classifier training, we can synthetically augment the speckle dataset by applying small translations, scaling, and rotations that mimic environmental shifts. This “stress-testing” of the network promotes inherent resilience to similar perturbations in practice.
d) Ensemble classification: Combining the outputs of multiple independently calibrated classifiers (each trained on speckle patterns acquired under slightly different conditions) can average out residual errors resulting from transient fiber fluctuations.
By integrating the strategies outlined above, hopefully, it may significantly extend the stable operating window of our MMF-based system and ensure consistent recognition accuracy in practical, real-world environments.

1) In “High-Accuracy OAM Recognition with Ultra-Low Sampling Density,” Paragraph 2, the authors state that “SPDs are imposed on the CCD.” This phrase is ambiguous and is suggested to be further improved.

Thanks for the kind reminder, we have carefully checked it and revised this sentence as follows:
“… a total of 9 points means that 9 such SPDs are imposed on the detecting plane …”
The modification can be found in Page 5 of the manuscript, marked with red color for your attention.

Response:
Thank you for the insightful comment. In response, we have carefully reorganized the Discussion section to improve the logical flow and coherence. Specifically, we revised the first sentence of Paragraph 2 to better align with the content that follows, and we eliminated redundancies in Paragraph 4 to enhance conciseness and clarity.
Additionally, we have incorporated some of the reviewer’s valuable perspectives into the revised text to strengthen the overall discussion.
These revisions are reflected on Pages 14–16 in the Discussion section, with all changes clearly marked in red for your reference.
3) Figure 6 shows a clear trend between single-point speckle intensity and OAM order. Does this trend generalize to other types of input, such as handwritten digits or axicons shown in the manuscript?
Response:
Thank you for the thoughtful question. The trend shown in Figure 6 illustrates the evolution of speckle intensity by treating OAM1 and OAM2 as independent and dependent variables, respectively. Because this experiment involves two well-defined, orthogonal variables (i.e., different OAM modes), it is possible to generate a 2D intensity map that captures the full relationship between them.
In contrast, inputs such as handwritten digits and axicons represent single-variable classes. As a result, it is not feasible to construct a similar 2D intensity profile, since the input space is not defined by two controllable parameters. Instead, the speckle intensity evolution can only be visualized as 1D curves—one per category—based on the temporal or spatial sampling sequence.
To further investigate this, we analyzed the intensity profiles of the first four sampling points for different MNIST digit classes using SMPD. As shown in Fig. R9, only the digit ‘1’ exhibits a noticeable difference in intensity profile, likely due to its unique structure. For most other digit categories, there is no significant variation in single-point intensity, making it difficult to extract clear trends as seen in the OAM case.

## Paper

## Abstract

Orbital angular momentum (OAM) recognition of vortex beams is critical for applications ranging from optical communications to quantum technologies. However, conventional approaches designed for free-space propagation struggle when light passes through scattering media, such as multimode fibers (MMF), and often rely on high-resolution sensors with tens of thousands of pixels to record detailed intensity profiles. Here, by harnessing scattering media as intrinsic encoders rather than detrimental factors, we introduce a speckle-driven OAM recognition technique termed spatially multiplexed points detection (SMPD). This method extracts intensity information from a few spatially distributed points in a speckle plane, where object feature is naturally multiplexed, thereby transforming scattering from a detrimental effect into an efficient encoding mechanism while drastically reducing sampling requirements. Remarkably, it achieves over 99% retrieval accuracy for OAMs recognition using just 16 sampling points, corresponding to a sampling density of 0.024% compared with conventional imaging-based approaches. Furthermore, spatiotemporally interleaved vortex beams decoding, high-capacity OAM-multiplexed communication, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST classification are implemented to verify the versatility of SMPD. This work establishes a scalable strategy for efficient optical information processing and fiber-based sensing in complex environments.

---

## Introduction

The precise manipulation of light’s orbital angular momentum (OAM) phase dependence of exp(iℓθ), enables robust encoding of information into discrete OAM modes. These modes form the backbone of spatial multiplexing strategies that transcend classical transmission limits1–3.

To decode OAM modes, approaches such as interferometry19–21, vortex diffraction grating22–24, and machine learning25,26 have proven effective in free-space environments. While demonstrating success, they generally depend on high-resolution imaging to capture well-defined full-field light structures, necessitating thousands of pixels or more and computationally intensive processing. Such reliance on dense spatial sampling imposes stringent trade-offs; it throttles system bandwidth, complicates scalability, and obstructs real-time operation27,28. Consequently, applications demanding compact form factors, high-speed detection, or operation in photon-limited scenarios, cornerstones of next-generation photonic technologies, remain largely out of reach.

Recent advances reveal that the ostensibly disordered nature of speckle fields marks a profound redundancy in their information content29–31. Unlike direct imaging systems, which localize spatial information to discrete regions, multiple scattering in complex media redistributes input-field contributions across the entire speckle pattern (see Supplementary Note 1 for more details). This non-local encoding enables information retrieval based on partial-field sampling for tasks such as imaging through scattering media32, diffuser-based super-resolution imaging via sub-Nyquist sampling33, and OAM recognition5,9,34–36 from arbitrary speckle subregions.

Yet, leveraging this redundancy for ultra-low-sampling detection remains underexplored. Although indeed utilizing a portion of the speckle field, current implementations still often rely on capturing a high-resolution intensity profile pattern (comprising thousands to millions of data points). A pivot challenge persists: What constitutes the minimal spatial sampling required to maintain accurate, scalable mode discrimination?

To address this, we propose spatially multiplexed points detection (SMPD), a framework for single-shot pattern classification with unprecedented sampling efficiency. Instead of recording full-field speckles, SMPD spatially samples intensity fluctuations at a sparse array of spatially multiplexed single-pixel detectors (SPDs), each capturing globally encoded information from the scattered field. A custom-designed neural network deciphers these sub-Nyquist intensity sequences, achieving robust OAM recognition with a sampling density of 0.024%, 4096 times lower than conventional imaging-based methods, while maintaining over 99% accuracy in diversity OAM recognition scenarios. Beyond OAM-mode retrieval, SMPD generalizes to classify mode-dependent features and distinguish complex optical fields, including handwritten digit recognition, grayscale images of clothing classification, and axicon angle identification, demonstrating its versatility across diverse scenarios.

By refining the spatial sampling-information capability trade-off, SMPD transcends the limitation of imaging-centric detection paradigms. This approach enables high-dimensional optical sensing and communication systems that are both compact and bandwidth-efficient, critical for real-time operation in photon-starved environments. Furthermore, its ultralow sampling requirements may unlock applications for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) sensing, low-power LIDAR, and quantum-enhanced sensing, where conventional pixel-dense sensors, constrained by their limited bandwidth and spectral ranges, prove impractical. SMPD thus establishes a pathway toward scalable photonic technologies, bridging the gap between theoretical information redundancy and practical, resource-efficient detection.

---

## Results

The proposed SMPD framework was rigorously evaluated through a series of experiments to validate its efficiency in various complex scenarios of OAM recognition and its applicability to pattern classification. Below, we present the key findings that highlight the method’s performance, robustness, and scalability.

High-accuracy OAMs recognition with ultra-low sampling density
Figure 1 illustrates the concept of SMPD, where two orthogonally polarized vortex beams transmitted through a multimode fiber (MMF) generate a speckle pattern at the distal end of the fiber. Instead of conventional full-field imaging, SMPD employs spatially distributed SPDs to sample sparse intensity points. These measurements are processed by a customized neural network termed as Recognizing OAM Artificial Neural Network (ROAM-ANN), which secures two paths to extract the features of the inputs in different dimensions and eventually outputs the encoded OAMs from the pointwise intensity sequences.

To quantify the impact of SPD parameters on recognition accuracy, we systematically varied the number and size of SPDs (Fig. 2). A charge-coupled device (CCD) camera with various masks was used to create different SPDs of varying numbers and sizes. Here, SPD is defined in units of ‘px’, and 1 px corresponds to the area of a single element (7.42 μm2) in the CCD camera. For instance, an SPD area of 52 px indicates 5 by 5 neighboring CCD elements are combined to form one SPD, and a total of 9 points mean that 9 such SPDs are imposed on the detecting plane via the mask. For each SPD, the light intensities detected by CCD’s light-sensitive elements are accumulated, and the recorded intensity sequence of the SPD array is used as the input of the network.

The recognition results for the test sets, each containing 1000 intensity sequences randomly selected from a dataset of 10,000 combinations of two orthogonally polarized vortex beams (both OAMs varying from 1 to 10.9 with an interval of 0.1) and excluded from the training process, are shown in Fig. 2a (more detailed results can be found in Supplementary Note 2). As seen, 16 SPDs (each spanning 30 × 30 px) achieved >99% accuracy for both OAM modes. Critically, the total sampling density of this configuration is approximately 0.024% (16 vs. 256 × 256), corresponding to 4096 times lower than that of conventional imaging-based methods9 that usually require 256 × 256 or more pixel arrays. Even with SPDs reduced to 2 × 2 px (retaining 16 detectors), accuracy remained above 93%.

That said, a clear trade-off emerged between SPD count and SPD size: reducing either the number of sampling points (which is critical for capturing multiplexed information and speckle correlations) or the sensing area (which helps resist perturbations and avoids sampling low-intensity or uninformative zones, as further discussed in Supplementary Note 1.4) led to degraded performance. For instance, with only 6 SPDs (1 × 1 px), accuracy dropped below 50%, highlighting the necessity of using sufficient sampling points and an adequately large sensing area to ensure robust performance, mitigate noise, and reduce sensitivity to pixel displacement. To better visualize this trend, Fig. 2b plots recognition accuracy as a function of the total SPD area across different measurement sets.

In addition to recognizing orthogonally polarized vortex beams, we also conducted simulations involving pairs of linearly polarized vortex beams with varying polarization angle differences (see details in Supplementary Note 6). The proposed method successfully distinguished overlapping vortex beams with polarization angle differences as small as 5°, achieving a recognition accuracy of approximately 90%. As the angular separation decreased to 3°, the recognition accuracy declined to around 80%, reflecting the increasing challenge of resolving nearly co-polarized beams. These results further demonstrate the sensitivity and robustness of our method in scenarios involving subtle polarization differences. It indicates that multiplexing OAM inputs across different polarization states in polarization space, combined with the proposed SMPD method, can largely reduce the amount of stored data while significantly improving the channel capacity of OAM transmission. This approach enables the potential for ultra-large capacity OAM transmission.

Spatial deployment flexibility
A key advantage of SMPD lies in its insensitivity to the spatial deployment of SPDs. As shown in Table 1, three distinct spatial deployments of 9 SPDs (with a fixed total area of 10 × 10 px) yielded minimal accuracy fluctuations: 89.40–95.15% for OAM1 and 78.05-80.55% for OAM2. This flexibility arises from the non-local encoding of information inherent to speckle patterns, where each SPD integrates contributions from the entire input field.

While our experimental results indicate that more sparsely distributed sampling regions yield slightly higher reconstruction accuracy than densely clustered ones, despite having the same number of sampling points and total area, this advantage is not absolute. Specifically, under conditions of strong scattering, where the information content can be fully scrambled and uniformly distributed across the speckle field, the choice of sampling region configuration (dense or sparse) has minimal effect on recognition accuracy (see details in Supplementary Note 1.4).

However, in practical scenarios, such as with speckles generated by a small-core MMF, a strong scrambled condition is difficult to achieve. In these cases, the speckle patterns exhibit larger grain sizes, leading to high redundancy in proximal sampling. Sparse sampling, by contrast, collects information from more uncorrelated regions of the speckle field and thus significantly improves reconstruction accuracy.

Crucially, sparse sampling shows robust performance across different scattering regimes. It remains effective whether the speckle grains are large (indicative of insufficient scattering) or small (indicative of strong scattering), offering broad applicability and better practical performance under varying physical conditions.

Spatiotemporally interleaved OAMs decoding via SMPD
Figure 3 illustrates the conceptual framework of the experiment (see Supplementary Note 3 for details). Each vortex beam, carrying a randomly selected OAM value alongside its corresponding temporal phase masks, is transmitted through the MMF in chronological order. At the distal end of the MMF, a CCD camera captures a single speckle image representing the superposition of the eight individual speckle patterns. This process is synchronized using a function generator, which triggers the digital micromirror device (DMD) eight times and the camera once during each acquisition cycle.

To enable single-pixel detection, eight masks with varying point densities (ranging from 20 to 49 points) are applied to the speckle patterns, effectively serving as virtual SPDs arrays, with each SPD covering an area of 10 × 10 pixels. Notably, the densest mask (7 × 7 SPD array, 49 sampling points) corresponds to just 0.07% of the 256 × 256 speckle image. Using this configuration, 20,000 speckle-label pairs were collected, each containing eight OAM values randomly selected from the 2.1~2.8 range. These data were split into training, validation, and testing sets in an 8:1:1 ratio, and processed through a modified ROAM-ANN (see Supplementary Note 4).

Figure 4 presents recognition performance under various sampling conditions, reporting both collective and individual OAM detection accuracy, as well as test loss. Collective recognition accuracy refers to the success rate of correctly identifying all OAM values within a single multi-OAM input. In this context, an input consists of eight distinct OAM modes, and a prediction is considered correct only if all eight are accurately classified. Using 49 sampling points (i.e., a 7 × 7 SPD array), the collective recognition accuracy reaches 98.6%, indicating highly reliable multi-mode detection. Individual recognition accuracy, on the other hand, measures the accuracy of identifying each OAM value independently, regardless of the correctness of other values in the same input. Under the same 49-point sampling configuration, the individual recognition accuracy achieves 99.82%, with only 28 misclassifications out of 16,000 individual OAM values in the test set. Even under more constrained conditions, using only 20 sampling points, the method maintains a robust individual recognition accuracy of approximately 85%, demonstrating strong performance even with limited spatial information.

High-capacity optical communication via SMPD
To demonstrate real-world applicability, we implemented an OAM-multiplexed optical communication system (Fig. 5). Two spiral phase images (100 × 100 pixels, 8-bit color depth) were encoded using OAM bases ranging from 2.1~2.8 and multiplexed via the optimized Lee hologram37 (see Supplementary Note 5 for details). A DMD was employed to effectively generate multiplexed vortex beams carrying the encoded data, which were then coupled into the MMF. As the beams propagated through the MMF, speckle patterns formed at the distal end. At the receiver, SMPD decoded speckle patterns using three configurations: 16, 9, or 4 SPDs. With 16 SPDs (10 × 10 px each), decoding error rates remained <0.2% (Fig. 5c). Reducing SPD size to 1 × 1 px slightly increased errors (due to localized noise and pixel displacement) but maintained robust performance. Even with only 4 SPDs (10 × 10 px each), the system achieved 74% accuracy, underscoring SMPD’s resilience under extreme under-sampling. This experiment validates SMPD’s potential for high-speed, low-bandwidth optical communication, particularly in resource-limited settings.

Generalizable pattern recognition via ultra-sparse speckle sampling
To demonstrate SMPD’s versatility beyond OAM retrieval, we extended its application to handwritten-digit and clothing classification using the MNIST dataset (Binary images)38 and Fashion-MNIST dataset (8-bit grayscale images)39.

Conventional speckle-based digit classification relies on high-resolution speckle imaging and computationally intensive spatial feature extraction. In contrast, as illustrated in Fig. 6a, SMPD employed simulated scattering transmission of MNIST digits or Fashion-MNIST (28 × 28 pixels), generating speckle patterns (256 × 256 pixels) that were subsampled via programmable SPD arrays. Three configurations were tested for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST: 7 × 7, 6 × 6, and 5 × 5 SPD arrays, where each detector integrated intensity over a 10 × 10 px region. This resulted in sparse sequences of 49, 36, or 25 intensity values per image. For both datasets, the 60,000 images were partitioned into training, validation, and test sets in an 8:1:1 ratio, and processed through a modified ROAM-ANN (see Supplementary Note 4).

Remarkably, SMPD achieved 92%, 89.45%, and 83.28% recognition accuracy on the MNIST test dataset (6000 samples) for 7 × 7, 6 × 6, and 5 × 5 SPD arrays, respectively (Fig. 6b). The confusion matrix (Fig. 6c) reveals minimal misclassification trends, with errors predominantly occurring between morphologically similar digits (e.g., 3 ↔ 5, 4 ↔ 9).

For the more visually complex Fashion-MNIST dataset, SMPD achieved test accuracies of approximately 84%, 82%, and 81% for each SPD configuration. As shown in the confusion matrix (Fig. 6c), misclassifications were concentrated among upper-body garments (such as shirts, T-shirts, pullovers, and coats), whose silhouettes exhibit high visual similarity; representative examples are highlighted in Fig. 6a.

These results confirm that spatially sparse, non-locally encoded speckle measurements encapsulate sufficient information for high-accuracy classification across diverse, non-orthogonal image sets, without resorting to pixel-dense sensors. By reducing sensor-pixel requirements to a low subsampling rate (e.g., 5 × 5 arrays vs. 28 × 28 pixels, 3.19% sampling density), SMPD offers a computationally efficient, hardware-lean pathway to deploy optical classifiers in scenarios where pixel-dense cameras are impractical or where speed, power, and footprint are at a premium.

## Methods

Speckle generation of orthogonally polarized vortex beams
A polarized femtosecond laser passes through a half-wave plate to adjust its polarization to 45°. A polarizing beam splitter (PBS) divides the 45° polarized beam into two orthogonally polarized paths. Each path is independently modulated by a spatial light modulator (SLM) to generate vortex beams with different OAMs. Then, the vortex beams are recombined by the PBS and coupled into an MMF using a 10× objective. At the distal end of the fiber, speckle patterns are collected by a 20× objective and recorded by a CCD camera (7.4µm pixel size). (More details can be found in Supplementary Materials Note 2).

Speckle generation of Spatiotemporally interleaved OAMs
Eight vortex beams carrying OAM values (ℓ=2.1–2.8) are sequentially modulated by a DMD illuminated with a continuous-wave laser. Each vortex beam is generated by Lee hologram37 and temporally modulated by a distinct chronological mask, and subsequently coupled into an MMF through a 10× objective. The output speckle field is collected by a 20× objective lens and recorded by a CCD camera. The entire process is synchronized using a function generator, ensuring temporal alignment between DMD modulation and CCD exposure. During each speckle acquisition period, the CCD remains continuously exposed to integrate the intensity of the speckle field generated by the eight sequentially transmitted vortex beams.

Multiplexed OAM transmission and speckle generation
A continuous-wave laser is expanded and directed onto the DMD, which sequentially displays the CGHs corresponding to the encoded gray values. The modulated beam is relayed through the 4f system and coupled into an MMF using a collimator. The output field is collected by a 20× objective lens and recorded by a CCD camera. In the data acquisition process, the DMD sequentially loads CGHs corresponding to grayscale values ranging from 0 to 255, each repeated ten times to improve signal stability. Two spiral phase images of 100 × 100 pixels are encoded into 20,000 CGHs, forming the testing dataset. To further mitigate environmental noise, all CGHs associated with grayscale values 0–255 are re-captured in ten repetitions after image transmission. In total, 5120 intensity-label pairs constitute the training dataset, while 20,000 CGHs serve as the testing set for evaluating multiplexed-OAM transmission (More details can be found in Supplementary Materials Note 5).

Speckle transformation of MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets
To numerically simulate the optical speckle transformation of standard image datasets, we modeled a transmission process through a random scattering medium using a complex-valued transmission matrix. Each 28 × 28 pixels image from the MNIST38 or Fashion-MNIST39 datasets was first vectorized into a column vector and normalized to the range [0, 1]. A random complex-valued transmission matrix T (with row of 282 rows and column of 2562) was then generated to represent the scattering process. The resulting out field (256 × 256) was obtained by multiplying T with the input image vector, treating the normalized values as the input amplitudes. The speckle intensity pattern was calculated as the squared magnitude of this complex field. Finally, the speckle intensity was partitioned into a grid of localized regions (5 × 5, 6 × 6, or 7 × 7), and the summed intensity within each region was used as a representative feature vector.

Neural network architecture and training
A dual-path neural network (ROAM-ANN) is designed to extract both local and global correlations within the intensity sequences. One path employs multiple 1D convolutional layers to capture spatially associated features, while the other uses fully connected layers to extract distributed sequence characteristics. The features from both paths are concatenated and fed into output modules with softmax activation. The network was implemented in TensorFlow 2.6 and trained with the Adam optimizer using binary cross-entropy loss. All experiments were performed on an NVIDIA P620 (More details can be found in Supplementary Note 4).

### Reviewer 1

The authors present a method for detecting OAM states of light using speckle patterns produced when superpositions of OAM modes, marked with polarization states, are transmitted through a multimode fiber. The method exploits sampling of judiciously selected points in the output pattern. While the methods and techniques, as well as supporting results, seem promising, I don't see any significant advancements either than incrementing to their previous iteration of the work as reported in Chinese Optics Letters, titled “Recognizing the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of vortex beams from speckle patterns”, where even the example images in their Fig. 5 (above SLM1) also appears in the previous article – same image, different colourmap. Similarly, work around the same theme was published [ J. Opt. Soc. Am. A 39, 759-765 (2022)] by Venugopal Raskatla in 2022, however, they applied the same method to LG and HG modes. Hence, this does not feel like original work, but rather an incremental effort, and cannot support it for publication in Nature Communications.
Moreover, crediting pixel density and sparsity for this performance can be misleading. By explicitly defining their sampling regions, but now in different areas, the authors are ultimately doing the same thing as using a small neighbourhood of pixels; strong scattering will ensure information redundancy across the speckle pattern. As long as the sampling satisfies the Nyquist criterion and the scattering is sufficiently strong, any selection of regions (in proximity or scattered) will contain the same information content.
Nonetheless, the fact that this method successfully classifies handwritten digits, whose optical encodings are inherently non-orthogonal, makes it especially compelling. Unlike OAM and polarization modes, these digit-shaped fields overlap in the transverse plane. Yet, the technique still achieves high accuracy, suggesting real promise for structured-light approaches to non-orthogonal image data. This has also been reported before.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the interpretation of pixel density, sparsity, and the role of sampling in our approach. We fully agree that, under the condition of sufficiently strong scattering, as long as the sampling satisfies the Nyquist criterion, any selection of regions—whether proximal or scattered—should contain comparable information content. This is a valid and important observation. That said, practical systems face constraints associated with a) sensor density within the sampling regions, which impacts local noise robustness, and b) spatial sparsity of the sampling regions, which helps mitigate redundancy by capturing uncorrelated speckle grains.
The reviewer’s opinion holds well in the idealized case of strong scattering, where speckle grains are small and densely distributed. But in scenarios involving insufficient scattering, such as with multi-mode fibers (MMFs) of small cores, the output exhibits larger grain sizes and proximal sampling becomes highly redundant. In such cases, scattered sampling significantly improves reconstruction accuracy, as it captures more independent speckle information. More importantly, scattered sampling is robust across both regimes: it performs well regardless the size of the speckle grains, thus offering broader applicability and better performance across various physical conditions.
We have incorporated both the reviewer’s perspective and our extended discussion—covering the influence of sampling density, spatial sparsity, and speckle characteristics—into the revised manuscript to provide a more balanced and comprehensive analysis. Detailed mathematical analysis and experimental validation are also presented in the following sections for your information: 2.1 Pixel Density within Sampling Regions, 2.2 Sparsity of Sampling Regions across the Speckle Field, and 2.3 Experimental Validation.
2.1 Pixel Density within Sampling Regions
There are two practical considerations that justify the use of higher pixel density in a given sampling region: noise reduction and sampling effectiveness in sparse speckle fields. In theory, a single pixel in each sampling region is effective. However, in practice, individual pixels are susceptible to noise from various sources, such as mechanical vibrations (causing pixel displacement) or sensor noise (e.g., dark current). Sampling over a denser pixel region helps to average out such noise, thereby increasing the reliability and stability of the recorded intensity.

As shown in Fig. S2a in the supplementary, the speckle field distribution is inherently random and sparse, with large areas exhibiting zero or near-zero intensity due to destructive interference. This sparsity means that if a sampling region is too small, there is a significant chance it may fall in a low-intensity or uninformative zone. A higher pixel density (corresponding to a larger active area) increases the likelihood of capturing useful information embedded in the speckle pattern.
Thus, while a single pixel may theoretically suffice, a higher-density (larger area) sampling region provides practical robustness and ensures greater information reliability, especially under real-world conditions.

Response:
We fully appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the classification of optically encoded non-orthogonal data, such as handwritten digits. Indeed, unlike orthogonal mode sets like orbital angular momentum (OAM) and polarization, digit-shaped fields significantly overlap in the transverse plane, making them inherently more challenging to distinguish. The fact that our method achieves high classification accuracy under such conditions demonstrates its robustness and highlights its potential for structured-light-based recognition in complex, real-world scenarios.
As mentioned in the additional simulations (1.3 Additional Experiments Part 1), the proposed SMPD method can successfully distinguish between overlapping vortex beams with a polarization angle difference as small as 5°, achieving recognition accuracy of approximately 90%. These results confirm that the proposed method is not only capable of recognizing digit-shaped fields but is also effective in resolving non-orthogonal structured-light fields with fine polarization variations. This reinforces the general applicability and robustness of our technique in complex optical encoding scenarios.
To further demonstrate the versatility of our method in non-orthogonal domains, we also conducted a simulation using the Fashion-MNIST dataset to classify grayscale images of clothing. Three configurations were tested for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST: 7 × 7, 6 × 6, and 5 × 5 arrays, where each detector integrates intensity over a 10 × 10 px region. This results in sparse sequences of 49, 36, or 25 intensity values per image. The dataset of 60,000 samples was split into training, validation, and test sets in an 8:1:1 ratio.
Remarkably, SMPD achieved 92%, 89.45%, and 83.28% recognition accuracy on the MNIST test dataset (6,000 samples) for 7 × 7, 6 × 6, and 5 × 5 SPD arrays, respectively (Fig. R8b). The confusion matrices (Fig. R8c) reveal minimal misclassification trends, with errors predominantly occurring between morphologically similar digits (e.g., 3↔5, 4↔9).
On the Fashion-MNIST test set, which contains 6,000 intensities sequences, SMPD achieved test accuracies of approximately 84%, 82%, and 81% for each SPD configuration. As shown in the confusion matrix (Fig. R8c), misclassifications primarily occurred among upper-body clothing items—such as shirts, T-shirts, pullovers, and coats—due to their high visual similarity, examples of which are illustrated in Fig. R8a.
These results confirm that spatially sparse, non-locally encoded speckle measurements encapsulate sufficient information for high-accuracy classification across diverse, non-orthogonal image sets, without resorting to pixel-dense sensors. By reducing sensor-pixel requirements to an extremely low subsampling rate (e.g., 5 × 5 arrays vs. 28× 28 pixels, 3.19% sampling density), SMPD offers a computationally efficient, hardware-lean pathway to deploy optical classifiers in scenarios where pixel-dense cameras are impractical or where speed, power and footprint are at a premium.

5. The recognition accuracy for OAM2 is consistently lower than that for OAM1 by ~10%. What causes this difference? Is it related to the intrinsic properties of the OAM states, their spatial frequency content, or potential overlaps in speckle features?
Response:
Thaks a lot for noticing the details. The observed difference in recognition accuracy between OAM1 and OAM2 can be attributed to a combination of experimental imperfections and slight misalignments in the optical setup. These differences are not primarily due to the intrinsic properties of the OAM states themselves, but rather to practical factors affecting the generation and coupling of the vortex beams.
Firstly, imperfections in the experimental components, such as the half-wave plate and polarizing beam splitter, contribute to discrepancies in the intensity and quality of the two vortex beams. Manufacturing tolerances and non-ideal optical coatings can result in uneven polarization modulation and splitting efficiency, which in turn causes variations in the output intensity of the two beams. Since the proposed recognition method relies heavily on the intensity distribution of the speckle patterns, such differences can lead to unbalanced datasets and reduced recognition performance for the lower-intensity beam—typically OAM2 in this case.
Secondly, the optical alignment of the two vortex beams introduces another source of asymmetry. The system requires independent modulation of each beam using separate spatial light modulators (SLMs), followed by coupling into the same MMF. This process involves multiple reflective and refractive adjustments, making it difficult to achieve identical coupling efficiency for both beams. Even slight deviations in beam alignment or focus can lead to differences in the resulting speckle patterns, further contributing to the accuracy gap between OAM1 and OAM2.
In summary, the lower recognition accuracy for OAM2 is primarily due to experimental factors. That includes non-ideal optical components and imperfect alignment during beam modulation and coupling, but not fundamental differences in the spatial frequency content or intrinsic properties of the OAM states. Addressing these issues through improved component quality and more precise alignment procedures may help reduce the recognition gap between different OAM channels.
6. Under the current experimental conditions, what is the finest OAM resolution (i.e., minimal discernible OAM spacing) that can be reliably achieved? What factors fundamentally limit this resolution?
Response:
Under the current experimental conditions, the finest reliably achievable OAM resolution is approximately 0.1. This means that the system can distinguish between two OAM states whose topological charges differ by as small as 0.1. In contrast, simulations suggest that the system has the potential to achieve an even finer resolution of down to 0.01 under ideal, noise-free conditions. In simulation tests where the topological charges of two vortex beams varied continuously from 1.00 to 1.99, the recognition accuracy reached 99.4% for OAM1 and 99.9% for OAM2, demonstrating the method’s theoretical capability to resolve extremely fine differences in OAM.
However, achieving this level of resolution experimentally is significantly more challenging due to the presence of noise and imperfections in the optical system. Under current conditions, a resolution of 0.1 represents a reliable and achievable benchmark for OAM discrimination.
7. When using 9 or 16 SPDs (with 1 px area), the recognition accuracy falls below 90%, yet the OAM multiplexed transmission accuracy exceeds 93%. The authors should explain this discrepancy.
Response:
This discrepancy arises primarily from two key differences between the experimental setups: light source stability and speckle grain size (SGS).
a) Light source stability
Experiment 1 employed a sub-femtosecond pulsed laser (Origami-10XP, 1028 nm central wavelength, 400 fs pulse duration, 1 MHz repetition rate). Experiment 2 used a continuous-wave (CW) laser (EXLSR-532-300-CDRH, Spectra Physics, USA). The former one, the pulsed laser, is inherently more sensitive to environmental fluctuations such as temperature, vibration, and power supply instability. These factors lead to variations in the average power and output intensity of the speckle patterns. Since the recognition method relies on ultra-sparse intensity sampling, even minor fluctuations can introduce inconsistencies in the dataset, degrading recognition accuracy. In contrast, the CW laser used in Experiment 2 provides a more stable output, leading to more consistent speckle intensity profiles and improved recognition performance. As a result, Experiment 1 requires more SPDs or a larger sampling area to compensate for the instability of the light source.
b) Speckle grain size (SGS)
As discussed in Responses 1–3, SGS significantly influences the recognition accuracy. In this study, Experiment 1 used a MMF with a 62.5 µm core diameter, resulting in larger speckle grains. Experiment 2 used a MMF with a 200 µm core diameter, producing smaller speckle grains. When the detector area is much smaller than the SGS, sampling becomes more susceptible to noise and less representative of the overall speckle pattern. In Experiment 1, the larger SGS reduces the effectiveness of sparse sampling with 1 px SPDs, leading to lower recognition accuracy. Furthermore, larger SGSs are generally more sensitive to positional shifts, reducing robustness in practical setups.
8. Given that multimode fibers (MMFs) are sensitive to environmental factors such as temperature and airflow, which reportedly limit data stability to ~30 minutes, the authors are encouraged to discuss potential mitigation strategies.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the practical limitations imposed by the environmental sensitivity of MMFs. Indeed, unmitigated fluctuations in temperature, airflow, and mechanical stress can alter the fiber’s transmission matrix and hence the speckle patterns, compromising data stability over extended periods. To address these challenges, we propose the following mitigation strategies:
a) Periodic reference calibration: By intermittently injecting a known reference beam (e.g., a Gaussian mode) and recording its speckle fingerprint, we can track slow drifts in the transmission matrix and apply a real-time correction to the classifier inputs.
b) Sliding-Window training: Implementing an adaptive classifier that continuously updates its training set using only the most recent data can compensate for gradual changes, effectively “retraining on the fly” to maintain accuracy beyond 30 minutes.
c) Data augmentation with perturbations: During classifier training, we can synthetically augment the speckle dataset by applying small translations, scaling, and rotations that mimic environmental shifts. This “stress-testing” of the network promotes inherent resilience to similar perturbations in practice.
d) Ensemble classification: Combining the outputs of multiple independently calibrated classifiers (each trained on speckle patterns acquired under slightly different conditions) can average out residual errors resulting from transient fiber fluctuations.
By integrating the strategies outlined above, hopefully, it may significantly extend the stable operating window of our MMF-based system and ensure consistent recognition accuracy in practical, real-world environments.
